_note: Hand fixes applied on top of the per-era research files.

facts: The AD 451 date marks the council, rather than an immediate complete institutional split.
Egyptian and Syrian opposition helped form lasting non-Chalcedonian churches.
Modern dialogues have found substantial agreement about Christ's divinity and humanity.

catholic.why: The largest Christian church, about 1.42 billion baptized members in 2024. Most Protestant traditions trace their separation from Rome to the Reformation.

anglican.sacraments: Two Gospel sacraments, baptism and the Eucharist. Baptism includes infants. Anglicans differ over counting five other rites and explain Christ's real presence in several ways.

pentecostal.sacraments: Usually two ordinances, believers' baptism and communion. Many distinguish Spirit baptism from conversion. Oneness churches link water and Spirit baptism to new birth. Some practice foot washing.

add.name: Eastern Catholic churches
add.summary: Eastern churches in communion with Rome, preserving their own worship and law. Brest in 1596 marks one reunion, not the beginning of all Eastern Catholic churches.
add.why: Catholic unity allows several Eastern rites, not only the Latin rite. Catholic and Orthodox churches still dispute the history of these unions.
facts: There are 23 Eastern Catholic churches alongside the Latin Church.
Maronites trace continuous communion with Rome. Other Eastern Catholic churches arose through reunions at different dates.
Many of them ordain married men as priests.
Each uses an Eastern rite such as Byzantine, Syriac, or Coptic.
add.sacraments: Seven sacraments, often called holy mysteries. Eastern tradition joins baptism, chrismation, and communion, including for infants. Practices differ across churches. Byzantine churches use leavened Eucharistic bread.
add.today: About 18 million in CNEWA's 2017 Annuario Pontificio figures
add.disputed: The 1993 Balamand dialogue rejected uniatism as a model for reunion, while affirming Eastern Catholic churches' right to exist.
